decks.title: The Living World — Part 1: Why we classify, taxonomy and the hierarchy
goals: Explain why living organisms need to be classified
Distinguish numerical taxonomy, cytotaxonomy and chemotaxonomy by the data each uses
Arrange the taxonomic categories in order and write the classification of man, housefly, mango and wheat

slides.heading: The Living World
slides.body_md: Part 1: millions of kinds of life, and how biologists bring order to them.

visual.alt: Flow from naming to grouping to showing relationships

slides.narration: Millions of kinds of organisms share our planet, and new ones are still being found. To study them, biologists first identify and name them, then place them into groups, and finally try to show how the groups are related.

slides.heading: Why classify living organisms?
slides.body_md: Without a system, every biologist would have to start again with each organism.

rows: A quick way to place it among known ones
Need to know how organisms are related
Groups that reflect resemblance and descent
Facts about a group apply to its members

visual.alt: Table of problems and what classification provides

slides.narration: Classification makes a huge variety manageable. A single scientific name ends confusion between local names, a newly found organism can be placed quickly, and what is known about a group helps us predict its members.

slides.heading: Taxonomy and systematics
slides.body_md: **Taxonomy** covers identification, nomenclature and classification. **Systematics** adds the study of evolutionary relationships. The word comes from the Latin *systema*, used by Linnaeus in *Systema Naturae*, published in 1735.

visual.alt: Flow showing that taxonomy plus evolutionary relationships makes systematics

slides.narration: Taxonomy covers three tasks: identifying organisms, naming them and classifying them. Systematics includes all of that and also studies how organisms are related by evolution. The word comes from the Latin systema, used by Linnaeus in the title of his book.

slides.heading: Modern branches of taxonomy
slides.body_md: Modern taxonomists use more than outward appearance.

rows: Many characters, each given equal weight and scored by computer
How similar overall are these two plants?
Number, shape and behaviour of chromosomes
Do two look-alike plants differ in chromosome number?
Chemical constituents such as alkaloids, flavonoids and proteins
Do two similar shrubs make the same chemicals?

visual.alt: Table of three branches of taxonomy with the data each uses

slides.narration: Numerical taxonomy scores many characters and gives each the same weight. Cytotaxonomy compares chromosomes, and chemotaxonomy compares chemical substances such as alkaloids and proteins. Together they supplement the study of form and structure.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: scoring characters
slides.body_md: Ten characters are scored 1 (present) or 0 (absent) for four plants. How similar are mango and neem?
bullets: Count the characters in which both plants score alike: **9** of 10.
Similarity = 9 divided by 10 = **0.9**.
Only one character differs: neem has compound leaves, mango does not.

rows: Grain fused with the fruit wall
Male flowers in a terminal tassel

visual.alt: Table of ten characters scored 1 or 0 for mango, neem, wheat and maize

slides.narration: Every character counts the same. Mango and neem score alike in nine of the ten characters, so their similarity is nine tenths. Only the compound leaves of neem set them apart.

slides.heading: Quick check: similarity
slides.body_md: Work out the similarity of wheat and maize from the table.
slides.narration: Quick check. Count the characters in which the two grasses agree.

slides.heading: Grouping by overall similarity
slides.body_md: Plants that agree in most characters are joined first. Mango and neem join at 0.9, wheat and maize at 0.8, and the two pairs only at 0.15.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: chromosome numbers
slides.body_md: Cytotaxonomy compares chromosomes. Bread wheat has 42 chromosomes in a body cell and its basic number is 7. What is its level of ploidy?
bullets: Divide the body-cell number by the basic number: 42 divided by 7 = **6**.
Bread wheat is therefore **hexaploid** (six sets).
Each gamete carries half the body-cell number: **21** chromosomes.

visual.alt: Table of chromosome numbers in body cells of six organisms

slides.narration: The body cells of bread wheat have forty-two chromosomes, built from sets of seven. Forty-two divided by seven gives six sets, so wheat is hexaploid. Chromosome counts like these help to separate species that look alike.

slides.heading: Quick check: ploidy
slides.body_md: What is the level of ploidy of a plant with 28 chromosomes in each body cell and a basic number of 7?
slides.narration: Quick check. Divide the body-cell number by the basic number.

slides.heading: The species concept
slides.body_md: The **biological species concept** (Ernst Mayr) defines a species as a group of interbreeding natural populations that are reproductively isolated from other such groups.

rows: Members mate and produce fertile offspring
Members do not exchange genes with other species
Cannot be tested for asexual organisms or for fossils

visual.alt: Table of ideas in the biological species concept

slides.narration: A species is a natural group that can interbreed and produce fertile young, yet is reproductively isolated from other groups. It is the basic unit of classification, although the idea cannot be applied to organisms that reproduce only asexually, or to fossils.

slides.heading: The taxonomic hierarchy
slides.body_md: Seven obligate categories run from **kingdom** down to **species**. Going down, organisms in a category become fewer and share more characters.

slides.heading: Four organisms classified
slides.body_md: Man, housefly, mango and wheat are the examples to learn.

visual.alt: Table of the classification of man, housefly, mango and wheat from kingdom to species

slides.narration: Man and housefly are both animals but separate at the phylum, chordates against arthropods. Mango and wheat are both flowering plants in the same division, but a dicot and a monocot, and so they separate at the class.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: how close are two organisms?
slides.body_md: Use the table to compare man with the dog (Canidae, Carnivora) and with the housefly.
bullets: Man and dog share kingdom, phylum and class: **3** categories; the lowest shared is the **Class**; they part at the order.
Man and housefly share only the **kingdom**: **1** category; they part at the phylum.
More shared categories means closer relationship.

visual.alt: Table of categories shared by man with dog and with housefly

slides.narration: Count from the kingdom downwards until the names differ. Man and dog agree down to the class, three categories. Man and housefly agree only in the kingdom. So the dog is a much closer relative of man than the housefly.

slides.heading: Quick check: shared categories
slides.body_md: How many categories do the housefly and a mosquito (Culicidae, Diptera) share?
slides.narration: Quick check. Compare the two classifications until they first differ.

slides.heading: Quick check: species idea
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about the species concept.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Classification gives a manageable, universal and predictive order to life.
Taxonomy = identification, nomenclature, classification; systematics adds evolutionary relationships.
Numerical taxonomy (equal weight, e.g. similarity 0.9), cytotaxonomy (chromosomes) and chemotaxonomy (chemicals) add data.
Species: interbreeding, reproductively isolated populations; the lowest category.
Hierarchy: kingdom, phylum or division, class, order, family, genus, species.

visual.alt: Summary table of branches and data

slides.narration: To recap: classification brings order to life. Taxonomy names and groups organisms, and systematics adds their relationships. Numerical, cyto and chemotaxonomy supply extra data. The species is the basic unit, and seven categories form the hierarchy.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: List the categories in the **correct order**; plants use **division**, animals use **phylum**.
Define **taxon** and **category** separately: a taxon is an actual group, a category is a rank.
Name the **data** used when asked to distinguish the three branches of taxonomy.
Show a **count of shared categories** when comparing two organisms.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Give the categories in order and use the right word for the second category. Keep taxon and category apart. Name the kind of data in each branch of taxonomy. And count shared categories when comparing organisms.

decks.title: The Living World — Part 2: Binomial nomenclature and systems of classification
goals: Write scientific names correctly following the rules of binomial nomenclature
State two advantages of scientific names over common names
Compare artificial, natural and phylogenetic systems by the characters each uses

slides.heading: Names and systems
slides.body_md: Part 2: how organisms are named, and the ideas that guide how they are grouped.

visual.alt: Flow from naming to artificial, natural and phylogenetic systems

slides.narration: This part has two halves. First, the two-word system by which every organism receives a universal name. Second, the three kinds of system that biologists have used to group organisms: artificial, natural and phylogenetic.

slides.heading: Binomial nomenclature
slides.body_md: Every species gets a **two-word** Latin or latinised name, introduced by **Carolus Linnaeus**. His *Species Plantarum* of 1753 came 18 years after *Systema Naturae*.

rows: Genus, a group of related species
Species epithet, which marks one species within the genus
Abbreviated name of the person who first described the species

visual.alt: Table of the parts of a binomial

slides.narration: Binomial means two names. The first word is the genus and the second is the species epithet. Together they name one species only. Linnaeus began using this system in the seventeen fifties, and it is now used worldwide.

slides.heading: Parts of a scientific name
slides.body_md: Take the mango, *Mangifera indica* Linn. Notice the capital letter, the small letter and the roman author.

slides.narration: The genus has a capital first letter and the species epithet a small one. The author is written in roman type after the name, often abbreviated. In print the two words are in italics. In handwriting each is underlined separately.

slides.heading: Rules of binomial nomenclature
slides.body_md: International codes set the rules; every scientific name must follow them.

rows: Latin or latinised, usually from a Latin or Greek word
Genus begins with a capital letter, epithet with a small letter
Handwritten: underline genus and epithet separately
Author name follows, in roman type and abbreviated

visual.alt: Table of rules of binomial nomenclature with examples

slides.narration: Remember four points: names are Latin in form, the genus starts with a capital and the epithet with a small letter, they are in italics when printed and underlined word by word when handwritten, and the author follows in roman type.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: correcting written names
slides.body_md: Three names were written wrongly. Correct each for a printed page.
bullets: **Homo Sapiens**: the epithet starts with a capital, so it becomes *Homo sapiens*.
**zea MAYS**: the genus needs a capital and the epithet small letters, so it becomes *Zea mays*.
**azadirachta Indica**: capital and small letters are both reversed, so it becomes *Azadirachta indica*.

rows: Genus not capitalised; epithet in capitals

visual.alt: Table of three wrongly written names and their corrections

slides.narration: Check the genus first: it needs a capital letter. Then check that the species epithet is all in small letters. Finally, set both words in italics for print, or underline each one separately in handwriting.

slides.heading: Quick check: writing names
slides.body_md: Decide whether the statement about handwritten names is true or false.
slides.narration: Quick check. How are the two words marked in handwriting?

slides.heading: Why scientific names are better
slides.body_md: A local name works in one place. A scientific name works everywhere.

rows: One name may stand for different species
Each name belongs to one species only
The genus word shows close relatives

visual.alt: Table comparing common names with scientific names

slides.narration: Common names change from place to place, and one name may even stand for two different plants. A scientific name is universal and unique, and it also tells us the genus, which hints at close relatives.

slides.heading: International codes
slides.body_md: Naming is regulated so that no two species carry the same name.

rows: International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi and plants

visual.alt: Table of two international codes of nomenclature

slides.narration: Two codes guide scientists. One covers algae, fungi and plants, and the other covers animals. They decide, for example, that the oldest valid name is the one that is kept.

slides.heading: Quick check: who named it?
slides.body_md: Complete the sentence about the introducer of binomial nomenclature.
slides.narration: Quick check. Think of the author of the book on plant species.

slides.heading: Systems of classification
slides.body_md: Over time, the basis for grouping organisms has changed.

visual.alt: Flow from artificial to natural to phylogenetic systems

slides.narration: Early systems used a single obvious character, such as habit or the number of stamens. Later systems used all natural resemblances. Modern systems try to follow evolutionary descent from common ancestors.

slides.heading: Comparing the three systems
slides.body_md: Learn each system by its basis, an example and its weakness.

rows: One or a few characters, such as habit or stamens
Separates related plants and joins unrelated ones
Overall resemblance in many characters, external and internal
Common ancestry, from fossils, anatomy, embryology and molecules
Depends on evidence that may be incomplete

visual.alt: Table comparing artificial, natural and phylogenetic systems

slides.narration: An artificial system, like that of Linnaeus based on stamens, is easy but misleading. A natural system, such as Bentham and Hooker, uses many characters. A phylogenetic system, such as Engler and Prantl, follows descent from common ancestors.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: one character or many?
slides.body_md: Use the four plants of Part 1. Group them first by a single character, then by overall similarity.
bullets: Artificial key on **compound leaves**: only **1** plant, neem, has them, so neem is separated from mango.
Natural grouping by all ten characters: mango and neem agree at **0.9**, so they go together; wheat and maize at **0.8**.

sections.heading: 2. Species concept and the taxonomic hierarchy
sections.body_md:
**Species.** The **biological species concept** (Ernst Mayr) defines a species as a group of **interbreeding natural populations that are reproductively isolated** from other such groups. Members mate and produce fertile offspring. The concept cannot be applied to organisms that reproduce only asexually or to fossils.

**Taxonomic categories** (the hierarchy) in descending order: **Kingdom, Phylum (Division in plants), Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species**. Each category is a **rank**; an actual group at a rank (for example the family Poaceae) is a **taxon**. Going **down** the hierarchy the number of organisms in a group **decreases** and the characters they share **increase**; going **up** the number of organisms increases and shared characters decrease.

| Category | Man | Housefly | Mango | Wheat |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Kingdom | Animalia | Animalia | Plantae | Plantae |
| Phylum / Division | Chordata | Arthropoda | Angiospermae | Angiospermae |
| Class | Mammalia | Insecta | Dicotyledonae | Monocotyledonae |
| Order | Primata | Diptera | Sapindales | Poales |
| Family | Hominidae | Muscidae | Anacardiaceae | Poaceae |
| Genus | Homo | Musca | Mangifera | Triticum |
| Species | sapiens | domestica | indica | aestivum |

The scientific names are *Homo sapiens*, *Musca domestica*, *Mangifera indica* and *Triticum aestivum*.

An actual group of organisms at any rank, such as Mammalia or Poaceae.
A rank in the hierarchy, such as genus or family.
A group of related species with more characters in common than with species of other genera.

sections.heading: 3. Binomial nomenclature
sections.body_md:
**Binomial nomenclature** gives every species a **two-word** scientific name. It was introduced by **Carolus Linnaeus** (*Species Plantarum*, 1753). Names are governed by international codes: the **International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi and plants** (ICN, formerly the Botanical Code) and the **International Code of Zoological Nomenclature** (ICZN).

**Rules**
1. The name is in **Latin or latinised** form, often drawn from Latin or Greek words.
2. The **first word is the genus** and begins with a **capital letter**; the **second is the species epithet** and begins with a **small letter** (*Homo sapiens*, *Triticum aestivum*).
3. In **print** both words are in **italics**; in **handwriting** each word is **underlined separately**.
4. The **author's name** (abbreviated, in roman type) follows the epithet: *Mangifera indica* Linn.
5. The oldest valid name has priority and no two species may share a name.

**Advantages over common names:** a scientific name is the **same in every country**, **unique** to one species, shows the **genus** (hence close relatives), and follows **fixed rules**, so scientists can communicate without ambiguity.

The second word of a scientific name, written with a small initial letter.
The abbreviated name of the scientist who first described the species, written in roman type.

sections.heading: 4. Artificial, natural and phylogenetic systems of classification
sections.body_md:
Biologists have grouped organisms on three different bases.
- **Artificial system:** uses **one or a few characters**, usually easily seen ones such as habit (herb, shrub, tree) or the number and arrangement of stamens (the sexual system of **Linnaeus**). It is simple, but it **separates closely related organisms and brings unrelated ones together**.
- **Natural system:** uses **all the natural affinities** among organisms, with **external and internal characters** from morphology, anatomy, embryology and chemistry. Example: the system of **Bentham and Hooker** (*Genera Plantarum*). It does not show descent.
- **Phylogenetic system:** groups organisms by their **evolutionary relationships and common ancestry**, using evidence from fossils, comparative anatomy, embryology and molecular data. Examples: **Engler and Prantl**, **Hutchinson**. Modern classification is mostly phylogenetic.

Using only the character 'compound leaves' separates neem from mango, though they match in 9 of 10 characters: this shows the weakness of an artificial key.

key_terms.definition_md: Classification based on one or a few easily observed characters.
Classification based on overall natural affinities in many external and internal characters.
Classification based on evolutionary relationships and common ancestry.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing *Homo Sapiens* (the species epithet must begin with a small letter) or underlining the whole name as one line.
- Calling the second category 'phylum' for plants (it is **division**; animals use phylum).
- Confusing a **taxon** (an actual group) with a **category** (a rank).
- Saying that numerical taxonomy weighs important characters more; every character has **equal weight**.
- Mixing up **natural** (overall resemblance) and **phylogenetic** (descent) systems.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark subparts: a term, an author, a rule, an example, a count of categories, a give-a-reason.
- 2–3-mark questions: classification of man, housefly, mango or wheat; rules with examples; three branches of taxonomy; three systems compared.
- 5-mark questions in parts: hierarchy with a classification and a trend; taxonomy with its branches and need; binomial nomenclature with corrections; the three systems with examples.

questions.stem_md: A herbal-products company finds that one root is sold under three different local names in three states, and that a poisonous look-alike is sold under one of those names. Which need for classification does this situation best show?

options.text_md: A universal and unambiguous way of identifying and naming organisms
A way of counting the cells in each organism
A method of proving that all organisms are alike
A way of breeding organisms in captivity

questions.solution_md: Different names for one organism, and one name for two organisms, show the need for a single scientific name and system of grouping — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A researcher scores forty characters of twelve grass species as present or absent, gives every character the same importance, and uses a computer to group the grasses by overall similarity. This approach is called

options.text_md: an artificial system based on one character

questions.solution_md: Many equally weighted characters evaluated by computer define numerical taxonomy — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Two shrubs look alike. A botanist finds that one has 16 chromosomes in its body cells and the other 24, and that their chromosomes differ in shape. Which branch of taxonomy has provided this evidence?
questions.solution_md: Chromosome number and shape are cytological data, the basis of cytotaxonomy — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Paper chromatography shows that the leaf extracts of two similar-looking herbs contain different alkaloids and flavonoids. A taxonomist uses this to treat them as separate species. The method is
questions.solution_md: Using chemical constituents such as alkaloids and flavonoids is chemotaxonomy — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The word systematics comes from the Latin word systema, which Linnaeus used in the title of his book
questions.solution_md: Linnaeus published Systema Naturae in 1735 — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In a numerical taxonomy study, the character “woody trunk” and the character “hollow internodes” are both scored 1 or 0. How are they treated?

options.text_md: The woody trunk counts more because it is easier to see
Both carry equal weight in the calculation of similarity
The hollow internodes count more because they are internal
Characters of the stem are ignored

questions.solution_md: Numerical taxonomy gives every character the same weight — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
Ten characters of two grasses are scored 1 (present) or 0 (absent). Each character counts equally.

| Character | Wheat | Maize |
|---|---|---|
| Woody trunk | 0 | 0 |
| One cotyledon in the seed | 1 | 1 |
| Parallel venation | 1 | 1 |
| Compound leaves | 0 | 0 |
| Fibrous roots | 1 | 1 |
| Hollow internodes | 1 | 0 |
| Fleshy fruit | 0 | 0 |
| Grain fused with the fruit wall | 1 | 1 |
| Male flowers in a terminal tassel | 0 | 1 |
| Sheathing leaf base | 1 | 1 |

What is the similarity of wheat and maize (matching characters divided by ten)? Give a decimal.
questions.solution_md: They match in 8 of 10 characters: 8 / 10 = 0.8.

questions.stem_md: A plant has 28 chromosomes in each body cell and its basic (monoploid) chromosome number is 7. How many sets of chromosomes does it have, that is, what is its level of ploidy?
questions.solution_md: 28 / 7 = 4 sets, so the plant is tetraploid.

questions.stem_md: Bread wheat has 42 chromosomes in each body cell. How many chromosomes does each of its gametes carry?
questions.solution_md: A gamete carries half the body-cell number: 42 / 2 = 21.

questions.stem_md: In numerical taxonomy every character is given ______ weightage.
questions.solution_md: Equal.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In numerical taxonomy every character receives the same weight when similarity is calculated.

**Reason (R):** A computer can process a table with hundreds of characters for many organisms.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true, but the ability of a computer to handle many characters is not the reason for giving equal weight — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Two plants that look alike can sometimes be separated into different species by cytotaxonomy.

**Reason (R):** Related species often differ in the number or structure of their chromosomes.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the difference in chromosomes is the reason cytotaxonomy can separate look-alike species — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: A herbarium sheet is labelled with a scientific name and not with the local name alone.

answer.model_answer_md: A scientific name is **universal and unique to one species**, so every botanist identifies the plant without confusion.

questions.solution_md: Universal, unambiguous name.

marking_scheme.step: Universal and unique name avoids confusion

questions.stem_md: Complete the analogy: Numerical taxonomy : equal weight to every character :: Cytotaxonomy : ______

answer.model_answer_md: **Number, structure and behaviour of chromosomes** (cytological data).

questions.solution_md: Chromosome data.

questions.stem_md: Name the branch of taxonomy that depends on the chromosomes of an organism, and state two features of chromosomes that it uses.

answer.model_answer_md: The branch is **cytotaxonomy**. It uses the **number** of chromosomes (for example 42 in bread wheat) and their **size, shape and behaviour**, such as banding or pairing at meiosis, to separate species that look alike.

questions.solution_md: Cytotaxonomy; two features.

questions.stem_md: Name the branch of taxonomy that uses (i) the alkaloids and proteins of an organism, and (ii) many equally weighted characters evaluated by computer.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) **Chemotaxonomy**, which uses chemical constituents such as alkaloids, flavonoids and proteins. (ii) **Numerical taxonomy**, in which a large number of characters, each of **equal weight**, are coded and evaluated by computer to give overall similarity.

questions.solution_md: Chemotaxonomy; numerical taxonomy.

questions.stem_md: A new museum is classifying its collection of preserved organisms. Give three reasons why classification is necessary.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It makes the **very large variety** of organisms **manageable** by placing them in groups.
2. It gives each organism a **universal name**, so that biologists everywhere can identify it without the confusion of local names.
3. A **newly found organism** can be placed quickly among known ones, and the **relationships** shown by the groups let us predict its features.

questions.solution_md: Three reasons.

marking_scheme.step: Placing new organisms and showing relationships

questions.stem_md:
Ten characters of three plants are scored 1 (present) or 0 (absent), every character counting equally.

| Character | Mango | Neem | Wheat |
|---|---|---|---|
| Woody trunk | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| One cotyledon in the seed | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| Parallel venation | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| Compound leaves | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| Fibrous roots | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| Hollow internodes | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| Fleshy fruit | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| Grain fused with the fruit wall | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| Male flowers in a terminal tassel | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Sheathing leaf base | 0 | 0 | 1 |

Calculate the proportion of matching characters for each pair. Which two plants should be grouped first, and what does the result suggest about the third?

answer.model_answer_md: Matching characters: mango and neem **9 of 10 (0.9)**; mango and wheat **2 of 10 (0.2)**; neem and wheat **1 of 10 (0.1)**. **Mango and neem** have the highest similarity and are grouped first. Wheat is far less similar to both, so it joins them only at a **low similarity**, and is a distinct, more distant group.

questions.solution_md: Three similarities; first pair; third plant.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Give three reasons why living organisms need to be classified. [2]
(b) State the kind of data used in (i) cytotaxonomy and (ii) chemotaxonomy. [2]
(c) How does systematics differ from taxonomy, and from which word is it derived? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Classification makes the **large variety** of organisms manageable, gives each a **universal name**, and lets a **new organism** be placed and its relationships predicted.

(b) (i) **Cytotaxonomy** uses the **number, structure and behaviour of chromosomes**. (ii) **Chemotaxonomy** uses **chemical constituents** such as alkaloids, flavonoids and proteins, which may differ between look-alike species.

(c) **Taxonomy** is identification, nomenclature and classification; **systematics** also studies **evolutionary relationships**. It is derived from the Latin word **systema**, used by Linnaeus in *Systema Naturae*.

questions.solution_md: Reasons; three branches; systematics.

marking_scheme.step: (c) Difference and origin of the word

questions.stem_md: Two groups of beetles live in neighbouring valleys and differ slightly in wing colour. When released together in a large cage, they mate freely and raise fertile young. According to the biological species concept, the two groups are

options.text_md: two species, because their wing colours differ
two genera of the same family

questions.solution_md: Free interbreeding with fertile offspring places them in one species, whatever small differences they show — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which sequence lists taxonomic categories from the lowest to the highest?

options.text_md: Genus, species, order, family, phylum, class, kingdom
Species, genus, order, family, class, kingdom, phylum
Kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species
Species, genus, family, order, class, phylum, kingdom

questions.solution_md: The hierarchy rises from species through genus, family, order, class and phylum to kingdom — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Man, Homo sapiens, is placed in the order Primata. In which family is he placed?
questions.solution_md: The classification of man is Animalia, Chordata, Mammalia, Primata, Hominidae, Homo, sapiens — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which pair gives the correct class and family of the mango, Mangifera indica?
questions.solution_md: Mango is a dicot in the family Anacardiaceae — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Wheat (Triticum aestivum) and maize (Zea mays) are both placed in the order Poales. What is the lowest category that includes both?
questions.solution_md: They share kingdom, division, class, order and family (Poaceae), but their genera differ, so the lowest shared category is the family — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Of these taxa, which contains the largest number of organisms and has the smallest number of shared characters?
questions.solution_md: The kingdom is the highest category listed, so it holds the most organisms with the fewest shared characters — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is a taxonomic category (a rank) and not a taxon (an actual group)?
questions.solution_md: Family is a rank in the hierarchy; Poaceae, Primata and Insecta are actual groups, that is, taxa — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The figure shows the classification of the housefly, with five categories marked A to E. Which letter marks the family?
questions.solution_md: The taxa read Arthropoda (phylum), Insecta (class), Diptera (order), Muscidae (family) and Musca (genus), so the family is D — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A reference collection of plants has 3 families. Each family has 4 genera, and each genus has 7 species. How many species are in the collection?
questions.solution_md: 3 × 4 × 7 = 84 species.

questions.stem_md: The housefly is classified as Animalia, Arthropoda, Insecta, Diptera, Muscidae, Musca, domestica. A mosquito is Animalia, Arthropoda, Insecta, Diptera, Culicidae, Culex, pipiens. In how many categories, counted from the kingdom downwards, are the two placed in the same taxon?
questions.solution_md: They are alike in kingdom, phylum, class and order and differ from the family downwards: 4 categories.

questions.stem_md: State the biological species concept and give one limitation of it.

answer.model_answer_md: A **species** is a group of **interbreeding natural populations** that are **reproductively isolated** from other such groups. A limitation is that it **cannot be applied to organisms that reproduce only asexually**, or to **fossils**, where interbreeding cannot be tested.

questions.solution_md: Definition; limitation.

questions.stem_md: Write the classification of the mango from kingdom to species, giving the scientific name.

answer.model_answer_md: **Kingdom** Plantae; **Division** Angiospermae; **Class** Dicotyledonae; **Order** Sapindales; **Family** Anacardiaceae; **Genus** Mangifera; **Species** indica. The scientific name is *Mangifera indica*.

questions.solution_md: Seven taxa.

questions.stem_md: Write the classification of wheat from kingdom to genus and state why wheat and mango are separated at the class.

answer.model_answer_md: Wheat: **Plantae, Angiospermae, Monocotyledonae, Poales, Poaceae, Triticum**. Both are flowering plants of the same division, but wheat has **one cotyledon** in its seed (monocot) and mango **two** (dicot), so they are placed in different classes.

questions.solution_md: Classification; monocot against dicot.

questions.stem_md: Wheat (Triticum aestivum) and rice (Oryza sativa) are both placed in the family Poaceae. Name the lowest category they share, state whether they belong to the same genus, and explain why they belong to different species.

answer.model_answer_md: The lowest category they share is the **family** (Poaceae). They belong to **different genera**, *Triticum* and *Oryza*, so they are not in the same genus. They are also **different species**: the individuals of each interbreed and produce fertile young only with their own kind, and are **reproductively isolated** from the other.

questions.solution_md: Family; different genera; reproductive isolation.

marking_scheme.step: Family as the lowest shared category

questions.stem_md: Man and the housefly are both animals. Name the categories in which they are placed together, name the first category at which they are placed apart, and say what this shows about their relationship.

answer.model_answer_md: They are placed together in the **kingdom Animalia** only (1 category). They first part at the **phylum**: man is a chordate (Chordata) and the housefly an arthropod (Arthropoda). Sharing so few categories shows that they are **distantly related**, unlike man and the dog, which stay together down to the class.

questions.solution_md: Shared kingdom; phylum; distant relation.

marking_scheme.step: Parted at the phylum with the two names

questions.stem_md: Wheat and maize are monocots of the family Poaceae; mango is a dicot of the family Anacardiaceae. For each pair, name the lowest category shared and the number of categories shared, and state what this shows about their closeness.

answer.model_answer_md: Wheat and maize share **5** categories, down to the **family**; wheat and mango share **2**, down to the **division**, and so do maize and mango. The pair that shares the **more** categories also shares **more characters**, so wheat and maize are **closely related**, while mango is distant from both.

questions.solution_md: Counts; lowest shared; conclusion.

marking_scheme.step: More shared categories mean closer relationship

questions.stem_md:
(a) List the seven taxonomic categories in descending order, from the highest to the lowest. [1]
(b) Write the classification of man from kingdom to species. [2]
(c) State the lowest category that man shares with the dog (family Canidae, order Carnivora), and explain what happens to the number of organisms and the characters they share as we move from the kingdom to the species. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Kingdom, phylum (division in plants), class, order, family, genus, species.**

(b) Man: **Animalia, Chordata, Mammalia, Primata, Hominidae, Homo, sapiens** — that is, kingdom Animalia, phylum Chordata, class Mammalia, order Primata, family Hominidae, genus Homo, species sapiens.

(c) Man and the dog share the kingdom, phylum and **class (Mammalia)**: the **class** is the lowest shared category. Moving **down** from kingdom to species, the **number of organisms** in each group **decreases** and the **characters they share increase**.

questions.solution_md: Order; classification of man; shared class and trend.

marking_scheme.step: (c) Trend in number and shared characters

options.text_md: It is shorter than any common name
It describes the colour of the fruit
It can be changed by any author at any time
It is the same in every language and refers to a single species

options.text_md: The scientist who first described the species
The country where wheat was first grown

Both, since a mushroom is neither a plant nor an animal
International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi and plants

questions.solution_md: Linnaeus.

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: The same common name can be unsafe for identifying a medicinal plant.

answer.model_answer_md: One common name may be used for **different plants in different regions**, while one plant may have **many common names**.

questions.solution_md: Common names are ambiguous.

marking_scheme.step: Same name for different plants, or many names for one

questions.stem_md: State two advantages of scientific names over common names, using the example of the papaya, Carica papaya.

answer.model_answer_md: A scientific name such as *Carica papaya* is **universal**, the same in every language, whereas papita and pawpaw vary with the region. It is also **unique** to one species and follows **international rules**, so no other species can carry it.

questions.solution_md: Universal; unique.

marking_scheme.step: Unique to one species and rule-governed

questions.stem_md: A student writes “Homo Sapiens” in a printed article and, by hand, draws one line under the whole name. Point out the two mistakes and write the name correctly for print.

answer.model_answer_md: The **species epithet** *sapiens* must begin with a **small letter**, not a capital. In handwriting, the **genus and the epithet are underlined separately**, not with one line. In print the correct form is *Homo sapiens* in italics.

questions.solution_md: Capital in the epithet; one line under both.

questions.stem_md: State three rules of binomial nomenclature, illustrating each with the name of wheat, Triticum aestivum Linn.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The name has **two words, genus then species epithet**: *Triticum* is the genus and *aestivum* the epithet.
2. The **genus begins with a capital letter and the epithet with a small letter**; in print both are in **italics**, and in handwriting each is **underlined separately**.
3. The **author’s name**, abbreviated and in roman type, follows: **Linn.** shows that Linnaeus first described it.

questions.solution_md: Three rules with the example.

marking_scheme.step: Capital and small letters; italics or underline

questions.stem_md:
(a) Who introduced binomial nomenclature, and what does the word binomial mean? [1]
(b) State two rules for writing a scientific name, one for print and one for handwriting. [2]
(c) Correct these two wrongly written names for a printed page, naming the fault in each: zea MAYS and azadirachta Indica. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Carolus Linnaeus** introduced it; **binomial** means a **two-word** name, genus followed by species epithet.

(b) In **print** the name is set in **italics**; in **handwriting** the genus and the epithet are **underlined separately**. (Also: the genus begins with a capital letter and the epithet with a small letter.)

(c) *Zea mays*: the genus lacked a capital letter and the epithet was in capitals. *Azadirachta indica*: the genus lacked a capital and the epithet had a capital letter.

questions.solution_md: Introducer and meaning; two rules; corrections.

**Reason (R):** Linnaeus’s sexual system was a phylogenetic system.

answer.model_answer_md: It uses **one or a few characters**, so it **separates related organisms and groups unrelated ones**.

questions.solution_md: Few characters.

questions.stem_md: What is a phylogenetic system of classification? Name two botanists who proposed such systems.

answer.model_answer_md: A **phylogenetic system** groups organisms according to their **evolutionary relationships and common ancestry**, using evidence from fossils, anatomy, embryology and molecular data. It was proposed by **Engler and Prantl** and by **Hutchinson**.

questions.solution_md: Descent; two names.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between an artificial and a natural system of classification on the basis of the characters used, giving one example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: An **artificial system** uses **one or a few characters** such as habit or stamens, e.g. the sexual system of **Linnaeus**. A **natural system** uses **many external and internal characters** to show overall natural affinities, e.g. the system of **Bentham and Hooker**.

questions.solution_md: Characters used; examples.

questions.stem_md: Compare the artificial, natural and phylogenetic systems of classification, giving the basis of each in one line.

answer.model_answer_md: The **artificial** system uses **one or a few easily seen characters**, so it may separate related plants. The **natural** system uses **all natural affinities**, with external and internal characters, but does not show descent. The **phylogenetic** system uses **common ancestry**, shown by fossils, anatomy, embryology and molecular data.

questions.solution_md: Three bases.

questions.stem_md: Using the four plants mango, neem, wheat and maize, explain how a key based on the single character “compound leaves” would group them, and why this grouping is misleading when compared with the grouping by overall similarity.

answer.model_answer_md: A key on **compound leaves** puts **neem alone** in one group and mango, wheat and maize in the other. This is misleading because mango and neem agree in **9 of 10** characters (similarity 0.9) and are close relatives. Using **all characters**, **mango and neem** group together and **wheat and maize** group together.

questions.solution_md: Neem alone; misleading; natural groups.

marking_scheme.step: Mango and neem agree in nine characters

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define artificial, natural and phylogenetic systems of classification. [3]
(b) Give one weakness of an artificial system. [1]
(c) State one way in which a phylogenetic system goes beyond a natural system. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The **artificial system** groups organisms by **one or a few easily seen characters**. The **natural system** uses **overall natural affinities** in many external and internal characters. The **phylogenetic system** is based on **evolutionary relationships and common ancestry**.

(b) It **separates closely related organisms and places unrelated ones together**, because the few characters chosen may not reflect real relationship.

(c) It **shows descent from common ancestors**, using fossils, anatomy, embryology and molecular data, which a natural system based on resemblance does not.

questions.solution_md: Definitions; weakness; descent.

questions.passage_md:
A herbarium sheet lists six plants of a village.

| Scientific name | Family |
|---|---|
| *Ficus benghalensis* | Moraceae |
| *Ficus religiosa* | Moraceae |
| *Mangifera indica* | Anacardiaceae |
| *Oryza sativa* | Poaceae |
| *Zea mays* | Poaceae |
| *Triticum aestivum* | Poaceae |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** 5

**(b)** (a) Division

**(c)** (i) They share the **genus *Ficus*** and therefore the family **Moraceae** and all higher categories. They are different species because each is a separate natural population, **reproductively isolated** from the other, with its own epithet.

**OR** (ii) The lowest category they share is the **family Poaceae**. They are in different genera, *Zea* and *Triticum*, because each genus is a group of related species with **more characters in common** inside it than with the species of the other genus.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Ficus occurs twice, so the genera are Ficus, Mangifera, Oryza, Zea and Triticum: 5.

**(b)** The six plants include dicots and monocots, so they share only the kingdom and the division Angiospermae — option (a).

**(c)** (i) Shared down to genus; reproductive isolation.

(ii) Family; different genera.

questions.passage_md:
A botanist records the number of chromosomes in the body cells of three look-alike herbs. The basic number of the group is 10.

| Herb | Chromosomes in a body cell |
|---|---|
| P | 20 |
| Q | 20 |
| R | 40 |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** 4

**(b)** (b) Cytotaxonomy

**(c)** P and Q have the **same chromosome number** (twenty), so counting separates nothing. Other data could be tried, such as **chromosome shape** and banding, **chemical constituents** (chemotaxonomy) or **many other characters** scored for numerical taxonomy.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** 40 / 10 = 4 sets.

**(b)** Chromosome number is the data of cytotaxonomy — option (b).

**(c)** Same number; another data type.

children.stem_md: What is the level of ploidy of herb R?
The botanist uses the chromosome numbers to treat R as a separate species. Which branch of taxonomy is this?
children.solution_md: Chromosome number is the data of cytotaxonomy — option (b).

children.stem_md: Why can counting chromosomes alone not separate herbs P and Q, and what other kind of data could be tried?

answer.model_answer_md: P and Q have the **same chromosome number** (twenty), so counting separates nothing. Other data could be tried, such as **chromosome shape** and banding, **chemical constituents** (chemotaxonomy) or **many other characters** scored for numerical taxonomy.
